verses.text: Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.
For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries.
But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church.

I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied: for greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying.
Now, brethren, if I come unto you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you, except I shall speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine?
And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped?
For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without signification.
Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church.
Wherefore let him that speaketh in an unknown tongue pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in an unknown tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful.
What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
For thou verily givest thanks well, but the other is not edified.
I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all:
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men.
In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord.
Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe.
If therefore the whole church be come together into one place, and all speak with tongues, and there come in those that are unlearned, or unbelievers, will they not say that ye are mad?
But if all prophesy, and there come in one that believeth not, or one unlearned, he is convinced of all, he is judged of all:
And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth.
How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying.
If any man speak in an unknown tongue, let it be by two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret.
But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God.
Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge.
If any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace.
For ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted.
And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church.
What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?
If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord.
But if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant.
Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues.
Let all things be done decently and in order.

summary: The praise of charity turns immediately into instruction: "Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy." Both are commanded, but they are ranked, and the whole chapter explains the ranking by one criterion. An untranslated tongue is directed upward, since the speaker "speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries," while prophecy is directed outward, "unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort." The difference is stated as an audit: "He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church." Paul is careful to concede rather than forbid — "I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied" — and he adds the qualifier that governs the rest, "except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying." Then come the sound analogies. A pipe or harp that gives no "distinction in the sounds" communicates nothing; "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?"; unintelligible speech means "ye shall speak into the air." Every language in the world has meaning to someone, but "if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me." So the standard is fixed: "forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church." Paul applies it even to prayer. The tongue-speaker should "pray that he may interpret," because "if I pray in an unknown tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful"; his resolution is to do both — "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also" — since otherwise the hearer "that occupieth the room of the unlearned" cannot "say Amen at thy giving of thanks." The thanksgiving may be excellent, "but the other is not edified." He then plays his strongest personal card and immediately spends it against himself: "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all: Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue." A rebuke follows — "be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men" — supported by a citation, "With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord," from which Paul draws the conclusion that "tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe." He then stages the scene twice. If outsiders arrive while "all speak with tongues," the verdict is "will they not say that ye are mad?" If instead "all prophesy," the unbeliever "is convinced of all, he is judged of all: And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth." From there Paul legislates. The gathering he describes is fully participatory — "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation" — under one rule, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Tongues are limited to "two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret," and where there is no interpreter, "let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God." Prophets likewise speak "two or three, and let the other judge," yielding to one another so that "if any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace," because "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted." The theological justification is compressed into two clauses: "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" and "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints." Then comes the disputed instruction, "Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak... And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home." Paul closes by puncturing Corinthian exceptionalism — "What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" — claiming apostolic authority for the whole set of rules, "let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord," dismissing further argument with "if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant," and ending in balance: "covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues. Let all things be done decently and in order."
takeaways: One criterion runs through the entire chapter and settles every question in it: does the assembly understand, and is it built up. Paul states it as a command — "seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church" — and repeats it as the rule over the whole gathering, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Intelligibility is not a concession to the slow or the unspiritual; it is the criterion by which a genuine gift is evaluated in public. The trumpet image makes the stakes plain, since "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?" A signal nobody can read is not a superior signal but a failed one.

Paul never prohibits tongues; he ranks and regulates them, and he is scrupulous about saying so at both ends of the argument. He opens with "I would that ye all spake with tongues," claims "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all," and closes with the direct command "forbid not to speak with tongues." What he denies is that a private benefit is automatically a public one, since "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church." His own arithmetic is the sharpest statement of the ratio: "five words with my understanding" in the assembly are worth more than "ten thousand words in an unknown tongue."

Corporate worship is assessed by how it lands on the person who does not yet belong. Paul introduces two outsiders — the "unlearned" who cannot "say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest," and the unbeliever who walks in off the street — and the two outcomes he sketches could not be further apart. Untranslated ecstasy produces the verdict "ye are mad"; comprehensible prophecy produces conviction so exact that "the secrets of his heart made manifest," ending with a man "falling down on his face" to "worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth." A church's meeting is therefore a public act with evangelistic consequences, and self-absorbed worship forfeits them.

Inspiration, in Paul's account, does not suspend the speaker's responsibility. His rule that "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" means the gift is under the control of the person who has it, which is why he can command a prophet mid-flow to "hold his peace" when "any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by," cap tongues at "two, or at the most by three," and impose silence where there is no interpreter. This removes the standard excuse for disorder. Nobody at Corinth could plead that the Spirit had overridden them, because the Spirit does not produce what "God is not the author of" — namely "confusion."

Prophecy is also placed under judgement rather than accepted uncritically: "Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge." A word claimed as revelation is to be weighed by the assembly, not received simply because it was delivered with confidence. Paired with the discerning of spirits named in the previous chapter, this establishes that the New Testament expects inspired speech to be tested in public, which is as much a protection of the congregation as it is a discipline on the speaker.

The order Paul imposes is theological rather than merely administrative, and it is deliberately not a demand for silence. He grounds it in God's own character, "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace," appeals beyond Corinth to the practice of "all churches of the saints," and punctures their sense of being a special case with "came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" Yet the same passage envisions a meeting where "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation" and where "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted." The final rule, "Let all things be done decently and in order," is stated positively for that reason: the regulation exists to make broad participation possible, not to shut it down.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:4-11 — every man heard them speak in his own language... we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God
crossRefs.why: Pentecost is the founding instance of the gift Paul is regulating, and the contrast is the key to the chapter. There the tongues were immediately understood by foreigners and functioned as a sign to outsiders, exactly the role Paul assigns them when he says "tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not." At Corinth the same gift was producing the opposite effect, leaving hearers unable to say Amen, which is why Paul demands interpretation before it may be used in the assembly.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 28:11-12 — with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people... yet they would not hear
crossRefs.why: This is the text Paul cites as "in the law it is written," and its original setting explains the sober conclusion he draws from it. Unintelligible speech there is a judgement on a people who refused plain instruction, not a reward for the spiritually advanced. Reading the source passage shows why Paul immediately warns "be not children in understanding" and why he treats a church full of uninterpreted tongues as a sign against itself rather than a mark of maturity.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 11:29 — would God that all the LORD’s people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them
crossRefs.why: Moses refuses to restrict prophecy to an authorized circle when Joshua asks him to silence Eldad and Medad, and Paul's "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted" is the fulfilment of that wish under regulated conditions. The pairing shows that Paul's rules are not an attempt to narrow who may speak but a structure that lets many speak without the meeting dissolving.

crossRefs.label: Joel 2:28-29 — your sons and your daughters shall prophesy... upon the servants and upon the handmaids
crossRefs.why: The prophetic expectation Paul is operating inside explicitly includes daughters and handmaids among those who prophesy, which is why the silence instruction in this chapter has to be read against a wider background rather than in isolation. It also frames Paul's preference for prophecy as the characteristic gift of the age of the outpoured Spirit, available across the whole community rather than confined to a few.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 11:5 — every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered
crossRefs.why: Three chapters earlier Paul regulates how a woman prays and prophesies in the assembly rather than forbidding it, which creates the central interpretive problem of "Let your women keep silence in the churches." Any reading of chapter fourteen has to account for the fact that the same letter assumes women speaking prophetically in the same gathering, and the two passages are always argued together.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 2:11-12 — I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man
crossRefs.why: The pastoral instruction supplies the closest parallel to the silence passage and is the text on which the debate over its scope usually turns, since it links silence to teaching and authority rather than to speech as such. Whether the two passages restrict the same activity, and how broadly, is the substance of the disagreement between complementarian and egalitarian readings.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading holds that the charisms described here have never been withdrawn from the Church. Paul's regulations presuppose gifts in active use and he ends by commanding "covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues," which is read as a standing instruction rather than a temporary arrangement for the apostolic generation. Extraordinary gifts are understood as genuinely possible in any age, given freely by the Spirit and not confined to the ordained, but they are always ordered to the building up of the whole body and always subject to discernment by those charged with the care of the Church, on the pattern Paul himself sets when he tells the assembly to "let the other judge." At the same time the tradition treats the ordinary means of grace — the sacraments, preaching, and the settled life of prayer — as the normal and primary way the Spirit sanctifies, so that the extraordinary charisms are welcomed as supplementary and tested rather than sought as the measure of spiritual attainment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants are divided among themselves here more sharply than they are against Catholics. Cessationist readings hold that tongues and prophecy were revelatory sign-gifts attesting the apostolic message, pointing to Paul's own statement that "tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not," and argue that once the apostolic revelation was complete the gifts served no further purpose and ceased, as the previous chapter said they would; on this view continuing prophecy would compete with the finality and sufficiency of Scripture. Pentecostal and charismatic readings answer that the text sets no expiry date, that "forbid not to speak with tongues" is a plain command, and that Paul assumes tongues in private prayer where "my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful"; many hold tongues to be associated with a baptism in the Holy Spirit, and treat contemporary prophecy as non-canonical edification that must itself be judged by Scripture. Reformed and evangelical interpreters occupy a spectrum in between, often described as open but cautious. Every side agrees on what Paul actually legislates: whatever operates must be intelligible, limited in number, interpreted, judged, and directed at the edification of the church rather than the display of the speaker.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "Let all things be done decently and in order" establishes that public worship belongs to the Church as a body and is not the property of whoever feels moved. Paul does not merely advise; he legislates numbers, sequence, interpretation, and silence, and he closes the case with a claim of binding authority — "the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord" — while measuring Corinth against the common practice of "all churches of the saints." That combination of apostolic command and inter-church uniformity is read as the seed of liturgical order: worship is a received and regulated act, entrusted to the Church's pastors to arrange, in which the community's prayer has a shape that does not depend on the temperament of individuals. The "Amen" of the one "that occupieth the room of the unlearned" is heard as the congregation's own assent to a public thanksgiving, which is why the thanksgiving must be offered in words the people can follow.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants agree that order is commanded and that Paul writes with binding authority, but they divide over how far the chapter licenses developed ceremonial. On the regulative principle, only what Scripture positively warrants belongs in worship, so this chapter functions as a prescriptive list — reading, teaching, prayer, singing, thanksgiving with an intelligible Amen — and the burden falls on anyone adding to it. On the normative principle, whatever Scripture does not forbid may be ordered by the church in Christian liberty, which allows for liturgical development while keeping edification as the test. Many Protestant readers also press the picture in the middle of the chapter, where "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation," and argue that a service in which the congregation only listens is as distant from Paul's meeting as chaos is. Both traditions hold that worship is God-ordered rather than improvised, that it must be conducted in words the people can understand well enough to say Amen, and that its purpose is the building up of the assembly.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "Let your women keep silence in the churches" as a restricted rather than absolute prohibition, because the same letter has already regulated the manner in which "every woman that prayeth or prophesieth" does so, and Paul cannot be forbidding in chapter fourteen what he assumed in chapter eleven. The silence is therefore understood of a particular function in the assembly: most naturally the authoritative public judging of prophecy that Paul has just described in "let the other judge," together with the official liturgical proclamation and teaching that belongs to the ordained ministry. The tradition reads the passage as reflecting a real ordering within the assembly rather than a judgement on women's capacity, holding at the same time that women have genuinely received the charisms, have prophesied, have taught in many settings, and stand among the Church's greatest saints and doctors, while the sacramental office of presbyter and bishop remains reserved.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings split on this text as sharply as on any in the letter. Complementarian interpreters take the instruction as permanently binding in substance, restricting the authoritative teaching and the official evaluation of prophecy in the gathered church, and read it alongside "I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man," while agreeing with the Catholic point that chapter eleven prevents it from meaning total silence. Egalitarian interpreters press the same tension in the opposite direction and offer several accounts: that what is forbidden is disruptive interrogation during the meeting, which fits the remedy "let them ask their husbands at home"; that the instruction addresses a specific local situation of untrained hearers rather than a universal rule; or that the appeal to what the law "saith" is Paul quoting a Corinthian position which he then demolishes with "What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" A minority argue on manuscript grounds that the verses are a later insertion. All parties concede that the passage cannot be read flatly without contradicting 1 Corinthians 11, and all must give some account of how women prophesying and women keeping silence belong in the same letter.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
